scenes.narration: How can an expert let AI Agent do more? Ownership stays clear.
scenes.headline: Why do experts amplify agents?

scenes.narration: In June 2026, Anthropic published a privacy-preserving analysis of roughly four hundred thousand interactive Claude Code sessions from about two hundred thirty-five thousand people, observed between October 2025 and April 2026.
scenes.headline: Four hundred thousand sessions

scenes.narration: The pattern is not that experts micromanage every action. Stronger domain understanding is associated with longer action chains per instruction and a better ability to recover when the session goes wrong.
scenes.headline: Expertise enables delegation

scenes.narration: This episode turns the findings into a responsibility card: who owns planning, what execution is delegated, which evidence verifies the result, and who takes over on failure. The card is our practical synthesis, not an Anthropic template.
scenes.headline: Four-field duty card

scenes.narration: This video is packed with practical, high-value insights to help you get better at using AI. It is a longer one, so follow Tiny Agent and save it so you do not lose it.
scenes.headline: Practical high-value method

scenes.narration: Start with the observed division of labor instead of treating autonomy as a single on-or-off setting.
scenes.headline: Observe the real split

scenes.narration: The study separates planning decisions from execution decisions. Planning covers what to do, which approach to take, and what counts as done. Execution covers files, code, tools, and commands.
scenes.headline: Planning defines done

scenes.narration: In a typical session, people make about seventy percent of planning decisions but only about twenty percent of execution decisions.
scenes.headline: People own about 70% of planning

scenes.narration: The common pattern is simple: the person decides what to build, while the agent decides how to build it.
scenes.headline: Agents own about 80% of execution

scenes.narration: That does not mean one prompt and a silent exit. A typical session has about four back-and-forth turns, each offering a chance to correct direction.
scenes.headline: About four turns per session

scenes.narration: Each user prompt triggers around ten agent actions on average, and the distribution has a long tail. One check-in can therefore govern a substantial chain of work.
scenes.headline: Around ten actions per prompt

scenes.narration: The useful question is not how many steps the agent may take. It is which decisions must stay with the person who understands the problem.
scenes.headline: Every decision needs an owner

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, separate what to do from how to execute it.
scenes.headline: Separate planning from execution

scenes.narration: Second, delegate verifiable execution without giving away the goal.
scenes.headline: Delegate verifiable action

scenes.narration: Third, use staged check-ins to keep the direction correctable.
scenes.headline: Correct direction at checkpoints

scenes.narration: Next, understand why expertise can expand the agent role instead of shrinking it.
scenes.headline: Expertise expands action chains

scenes.narration: The study rates apparent task expertise on five levels using precise framing, requested verification, and who corrects whom. It is not a job title or a measure of general ability.
scenes.headline: Expertise is task-specific

scenes.narration: A senior engineer can be a novice in an unfamiliar language. An accountant who defines reconciliation rules and catches a month-end edge case can be an expert for that task.
scenes.headline: A domain expert need not be a coder
scenes.coreLabel: A domain expert need not be a coder

scenes.narration: In typical novice sessions, one prompt triggers about five agent actions and roughly six hundred words of output.
scenes.headline: Novice: about five actions

scenes.narration: In typical expert sessions, the chain exceeds twice as many actions, around twelve, and carries roughly thirty-two hundred words, about five times the novice output.
scenes.headline: Expert: about twelve actions

scenes.narration: After controls for work mode, task value, month, occupation, and model family, each expertise level is still associated with about nine percent more actions and thirteen percent more output.
scenes.headline: Actions and output rise by level
scenes.coreLabel: Actions and output rise by level

scenes.narration: More text is not automatically better. Precise constraints let the agent safely advance more checkable work before the next handoff.
scenes.headline: Constraints enable safe progress

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, expertise is specific to the task at hand.
scenes.headline: Expertise is not a title

scenes.narration: Second, precise constraints expand the agent’s useful action chain.
scenes.headline: Precision expands the action chain

scenes.narration: Third, judge progress by verifiable artifacts, not output length.
scenes.headline: Evidence beats word count

scenes.narration: Now divide responsibility by capability and uncertainty, not by drawing a simple human-versus-machine line.
scenes.headline: Allocate by risk

scenes.narration: Stable, reversible, rule-bound execution can be delegated in batches: reading files, making mechanical edits, running checks, and collecting evidence.
scenes.headline: Delegate reversible execution

scenes.narration: Goals, value conflicts, hidden constraints, and costly trade-offs stay with a person because they depend on domain context and consequences.
scenes.headline: Humans own goals and values

scenes.narration: When rules are clear but the environment is unfamiliar, let the agent investigate and list assumptions, then confirm the boundary before execution.
scenes.headline: Investigate unfamiliar terrain

scenes.narration: When failures repeat, evidence conflicts, or the affected scope expands, autonomy should decrease and responsibility should return to a person.
scenes.headline: Reduce autonomy on anomalies

scenes.narration: The observed Claude Code split is directional evidence from interactive coding sessions, not a universal ratio for every industry.
scenes.headline: The ratio is not universal

scenes.narration: Write decision types and escalation triggers on the card. Do not copy seventy and twenty as fixed operating targets.
scenes.headline: Write decisions and triggers

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, set delegation depth by reversibility and uncertainty.
scenes.headline: Use reversibility and uncertainty

scenes.narration: Second, keep goals, values, and costly trade-offs with a person.
scenes.headline: Keep costly trade-offs human

scenes.narration: Third, define the failures and conflicts that trigger a takeover.
scenes.headline: Trigger a timely takeover

scenes.narration: Turn expertise into observable responsibility actions rather than a vague claim that an expert is present.
scenes.headline: Make expertise visible

scenes.narration: A clear task definition names the object, constraints, completion evidence, and prohibited actions. A polished wish is not enough.
scenes.headline: Define a checkable task

scenes.narration: Write verification before execution: required tests, primary data, comparison checks, and the audit trail that must remain.
scenes.headline: Write verification first

scenes.narration: Expert users correct the agent at pivotal points because they can recognize fluent work that violates the domain rule.
scenes.headline: Correct pivotal deviations

scenes.narration: The study’s strict verified-success rate is fifteen percent for novice-rated sessions and roughly twenty-eight to thirty-three percent for intermediate or higher sessions.
scenes.headline: Verified success rises with expertise

scenes.narration: Most of the gain occurs between novice and intermediate. Working competence captures much of the benefit, while deep mastery adds a smaller margin.
scenes.headline: Most gains arrive by competence

scenes.narration: Experts also recover more often when sessions hit trouble. A responsible workflow needs a recovery path, not only a happy path.
scenes.headline: Design the recovery path

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, encode expertise as constraints and completion evidence.
scenes.headline: Encode knowledge as evidence

scenes.narration: Second, correct pivotal deviations instead of trusting fluency.
scenes.headline: Fluency is not correctness

scenes.narration: Third, preserve a path to diagnose, narrow scope, and take over.
scenes.headline: Preserve takeover paths

scenes.narration: Put the principles into a four-field agent responsibility card.
scenes.headline: Use the duty card

scenes.narration: Field one is the planning owner: who defines the goal, priorities, allowed trade-offs, and completion standard.
scenes.headline: One: planning owner

scenes.narration: Field two is execution authority: what the agent may read, change, run, and combine, plus actions that remain prohibited.
scenes.headline: Two: execution authority

scenes.narration: Field three is verification evidence: tests, primary sources, diffs, or reproducible commands attached to every consequential result.
scenes.headline: Three: evidence

scenes.narration: Field four is the failure owner: who takes over after repeated failure, conflicting evidence, scope expansion, or an irreversible action.
scenes.headline: Four: failure owner

scenes.narration: Fill the planning and failure owners first. Then open execution authority and close the loop by checking each required piece of evidence.
scenes.headline: Fill responsibility first

scenes.narration: This card is a workflow inference from the study’s division of labor and expertise signals. The report did not validate this specific card.
scenes.headline: An episode workflow inference

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, name the planning and failure owners.
scenes.headline: Name both owners

scenes.narration: Second, grant bounded execution authority.
scenes.headline: Then grant bounded authority

scenes.narration: Third, let agreed evidence determine whether the work is done.
scenes.headline: Evidence determines done

scenes.narration: Domain experts are effective with agents not because they make agents do less, but because they clarify goals, constraints, evidence, and takeover points.
scenes.headline: Expertise keeps responsibility

scenes.narration: Keep the research boundary visible. Success is inferred from transcript classifiers and verifiable signals, not real-world outcomes, and non-interactive usage is excluded.
scenes.headline: Research limits remain visible

scenes.narration: Before the next AI Agent run, write four fields: planning owner, execution authority, verification evidence, and failure owner.
scenes.headline: Write four fields before the run
scenes.coreLabel: Write four fields before the run

scenes.headline: Tiny Agent
